title: Top to bottom in a fresh session, with one command

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Hidden state is anything a script uses that the script itself did not make.

A script is tested for hidden state by running all of it, from the first line to the last, in a fresh session. A fresh session is a new R process whose workspace is empty. It has attached no package beyond R’s defaults. The one command for this is Rscript code/analysis.R, typed in a terminal whose working directory is the project root.

A script that passes this test also writes every result it makes into output/ with code. It sets the random-number seed with set.seed() before any random step. It ends with sessionInfo(), which prints the version of R and of every attached package.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Here is the trap with a script that works on your computer. While you work, R remembers. Every object you made, in the script or typed in the console, sits in the workspace. Every package you attached stays attached. Then a colleague runs it on their computer, where none of it exists, and it stops.

So test the script the way a stranger would run it. Start a new R with nothing in it, and run every line from the top. There are two ways to do that.

  • In RStudio, restart R (the menu Session, then Restart R), then run the whole script.
  • In a terminal, in the project folder, type one command: Rscript code/analysis.R.

The second way is the one to write in your README, because it is one line anyone can type.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a script that works for you and for nobody else. An hour ago, exploring the penguin file, you typed these lines in the console:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Then you tried a few things, and saved the line worth keeping as your script, code/analysis.R:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw |>
  count(Island)

Select all of it in the editor and run it. It prints the rows per island, because penguins_raw is still in your session from the console.

It works. Now run it the way anyone else would. Open a terminal in the project folder and type the one command:

Rscript code/analysis.R
Error: object 'penguins_raw' not found
Execution halted

Read the error literally. The new R has no object called penguins_raw. Nothing in the script makes one. In your session it existed because you typed the reading line in the console an hour ago. The script was never complete. Your workspace was hiding the gap.

Trisovic and colleagues reran R files that researchers had shared alongside published studies, and 74% failed to complete without error the first time they were run, as the last section showed. “Object not found” was one of the errors they met, and they write that it is “often related to missing files or incomplete code”. This one is incomplete code.

Fix it in the script, not in the session. Put the packages first, then the reading line:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(here)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  count(Island)

Run the same command again:

Rscript code/analysis.R
here() starts at ~/project
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Island        n
  <chr>     <int>
1 Biscoe      168
2 Dream       124
3 Torgersen    52

The same three counts, now from a script that makes everything it uses. Notice that Rscript printed the table without being asked. It prints what each line returns, just as the console does.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The fresh run catches what the script takes from your session: objects, attached packages, a working directory you set by hand. It does not catch what the script takes from your computer. A package that is installed on your computer and not on your colleague’s still stops the script on theirs, at its library() line. A different version of a package may run without any error and give a different result.

Rscript also stops at the first error. A script with three problems shows you one at a time. Fix it and run it again until it reaches the last line.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now the second trap: clearing the workspace by hand looks like a fresh start and is not one. The function rm() removes objects. rm(list = ls()) removes every object the workspace lists. Run it, then ask what is left:

rm(list = ls())
ls()
search()
character(0)
 [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:dplyr"     "package:readr"
 [4] "package:stats"     "package:graphics"  "package:grDevices"
 [7] "package:utils"     "package:datasets"  "package:methods"
[10] "Autoloads"         "package:base"

ls() prints character(0), an empty list: no objects. But search(), which lists where R looks for a name, still shows package:dplyr and package:readr. They are still attached. A script that forgot library(dplyr) would still find count() here, and stop on your colleague’s computer. Only a new R clears both. In RStudio that is Session, then Restart R, or Ctrl + Shift + F10, followed by Ctrl + Shift + S to run the whole script. In a terminal it is Rscript.

The same holds for source(). It reads a file and runs its lines in your current workspace, so a script run with source() can still lean on objects and packages you already have. Use it only straight after a restart.

Now make the one command produce everything. Two more things go into the script. The first is a random step. Suppose you want five rows picked at random, to check by hand against the field notebooks. The function sample() picks at random, and sample(344, 5) picks five of the whole numbers from 1 to 344. Each run picks different ones, unless you set the seed first. The seed is the starting point R’s random numbers are worked out from. See what it does:

set.seed(2026)
sample(344, 5)
set.seed(2026)
sample(344, 5)
set.seed(7)
sample(344, 5)
[1] 221 121 294  45 111
[1] 221 121 294  45 111
[1] 298 103 194 271 218

The same seed gives the same five rows. A different seed gives different ones. The seed is a number you choose and write in the script, so the next person gets your five rows, not their own.

The second is sessionInfo() as the last line. Here is the whole script:

# analysis.R: penguin rows by island, and five rows to check by hand
# Run from the project folder: Rscript code/analysis.R

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(here)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)

island_counts <- penguins_raw |>
  count(Island)
write_csv(island_counts, here("output", "island_counts.csv"))

# Five row numbers, picked at random, to check against the
# field notebooks. The seed makes the same five come out every run.
set.seed(2026)
rows_to_check <- tibble(row = sample(nrow(penguins_raw), 5))
write_csv(rows_to_check, here("output", "rows_to_check.csv"))

sessionInfo()

dir.create() makes the output folder if it is not there, and showWarnings = FALSE keeps it quiet when it is. Without that line the script would stop on a fresh copy of the project, where output/ does not exist yet. write_csv() writes a table to a CSV file, as in the section on summaries by group. tibble() makes a small table, here with one column, row.

Run it:

Rscript code/analysis.R
here() starts at ~/project
R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
Running under: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS

Matrix products: default
BLAS:   /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/blas/libblas.so.3.12.0
LAPACK: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/lapack/liblapack.so.3.12.0

locale:

 [4] LC_COLLATE=C.utf8     LC_MONETARY=C.utf8    LC_MESSAGES=C.utf8
 [7] LC_PAPER=C.utf8       LC_NAME=C             LC_ADDRESS=C
[10] LC_TELEPHONE=C        LC_MEASUREMENT=C.utf8 LC_IDENTIFICATION=C

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
 [1] utf8_1.2.4       R6_2.5.1         bit_4.0.5        tidyselect_1.2.0

[21] pillar_1.9.0     crayon_1.5.2     rlang_1.1.3      vroom_1.6.5

Nothing else printed, because the script writes its tables to files. Look in output/, and read one back as plain text. In the terminal, ls lists a folder and cat prints a file:

ls output
cat output/rows_to_check.csv
island_counts.csv
rows_to_check.csv
row
221
121
294
45
111

The five row numbers in the file are the five from set.seed(2026) above. Now read the record at the bottom of the run. The first line names R 4.3.3. Under “other attached packages” are the three this script attached, each with its version: here 1.0.1, dplyr 1.1.4, readr 2.1.5. Under “loaded via a namespace (and not attached)” are packages that are loaded but not attached. “Running under” names the computer’s operating system. Anyone who gets a different answer from your script can compare their own sessionInfo() with yours, line by line.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
sessionInfo() records the versions. It does not install them. A colleague with a newer dplyr can read that you used 1.1.4 and still have to find and install the old version by hand. Pinning versions so that another computer gets the same ones is what renv does, two rungs up. Recording every change to the script itself is version control, the next rung’s subject.

A seed makes a random step repeat on the same version of R. It does not make the five rows a good sample, and it does not promise the same five on a version of R whose random-number method has changed, as it did in R 3.6.0. That is why the seed and the R version are both recorded.

points.html: The error is to think that a script which runs on your computer is a script that runs. Before you send a script to anyone, run it with Rscript code/analysis.R from the project folder. Send it only when it reaches the last line.
rm(list = ls()) empties the workspace and leaves every package attached. source() runs a file in the workspace you already have. Neither is a fresh session. Restart R, or use Rscript.
When a script stops with “object not found” on someone else’s computer, look for the line that makes that object. Add it to the script, above the line that uses the object.
Put set.seed() with a number you write down before any random step: a random sample of rows to check, a random allocation, a simulation.
End every analysis script with sessionInfo(), and keep its printout with the outputs.
A number in your thesis that you typed from the screen has no line of code behind it. Write every table to output/ with code, and copy numbers into the text from those files.
A trainee says “it runs, I checked”. Ask how. If the answer is “I ran it in RStudio”, ask them to restart R and run it again in front of you.

One command in a fresh session tests the script against your computer only. It cannot show that a colleague with other package versions gets the same numbers, and it cannot show that the numbers are right.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, say what “hidden state” is. Name the one command that tests a script for it. Say why rm(list = ls()) is not enough.
blocks.answer:
Hidden state is anything a script uses that the script did not make. It may be an object typed in the console, a package attached earlier or a file made by hand.

The command is Rscript code/analysis.R, typed in a terminal in the project folder. It starts a new R and runs the file from the first line to the last.

rm(list = ls()) removes the objects and leaves the packages attached, so a script that forgot a library() line would still run.

blocks.prompt: Take the script you have been building through this book. Restart R, or open a terminal in the project folder, and run it with Rscript code/analysis.R. Fix every error in the script, one at a time, until it reaches the last line. Then make sure that it writes its outputs to output/ with code, that any random step follows set.seed(), and that it ends with sessionInfo(). Delete output/ and run the command again. Write the command into your README.
blocks.answer:
There is no single right script. Check yours against these:

  1. Rscript code/analysis.R, from the project folder, runs to the end with no error.
  2. Every library() line the script needs is in the script, at the top.
  3. The raw file is read in the script, with here(), from data-raw/.
  4. The script makes output/ if it is missing (dir.create()), and every table and figure is written there by a line of code.
  5. A seed set with set.seed() comes before any random step.
  6. The last line is sessionInfo().
  7. After you delete output/ and run the command again, every output comes back.
  8. The README’s “To rerun” line is that exact command.

If any of these fails, the script still depends on something outside it.

blocks.prompt: A journalist has three minutes. A research group has just been told that its published analysis “does not reproduce”. The journalist asks what that usually means, and whether it means the result is false. Answer them.
blocks.answer:
It can mean that someone took the group’s data and code and could not get the code to run, or got a different number. One study looked at R code shared on one research website. About three in four files did not run to the end without an error the first time. Common causes are dull ones: a file kept in a folder only the author had, a missing step, a package that has since changed.

So “does not reproduce” says that the analysis cannot be checked as it stands. It does not say that the result is false. It says nobody can yet show that it is true.

The quotable sentence: “If an analysis cannot be rerun, you cannot tell whether it is wrong, and neither can its authors.”

blocks.prompt:
Predict whether these lines print the same three numbers twice, then run them.

set.seed(11)
sample(10, 3)
set.seed(11)
sample(10, 3)
blocks.answer:
set.seed(11)
sample(10, 3)
set.seed(11)
sample(10, 3)
[1] 10  2  8
[1] 10  2  8

The same three, because the seed is set to the same number before each pick.

blocks.prompt:
Predict what the last line prints, then run all three. exists() asks whether an object of that name exists.

height_cm <- c(132, 141, 150)
rm(list = ls())
exists("height_cm")
blocks.answer:
height_cm <- c(132, 141, 150)
rm(list = ls())
exists("height_cm")
[1] FALSE

rm(list = ls()) removed every object, so height_cm no longer exists, and exists() answers FALSE.

blocks.prompt:
Predict what the last line prints, then run all three. Does rm(list = ls()) detach dplyr?

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
rm(list = ls())
"package:dplyr" %in% search()
blocks.answer:
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
rm(list = ls())
"package:dplyr" %in% search()
[1] TRUE

TRUE. dplyr is still on the list of places R searches. rm() removes objects, not packages. The operator %in% asks whether the text on its left is among the values on its right.

blocks.prompt: Write a script, code/analysis.R, that reads the penguin file from data-raw/, counts the rows of each species, and writes the counts to output/species_counts.csv. It must run on a fresh copy of the project, where output/ does not exist. Run it with Rscript, then show the file it wrote.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(here)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)

species_counts <- penguins_raw |>
  count(Species)
write_csv(species_counts, here("output", "species_counts.csv"))
Rscript code/analysis.R
cat output/species_counts.csv
here() starts at ~/project
Species,n
Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae),152
Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica),68
Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua),124

152, 68 and 124 rows, which add up to 344. These are rows of the file, one per nesting observation, not counts of birds. The dir.create() line is what lets the script run on a copy with no output/ folder.

blocks.prompt: This section’s last run of code/analysis.R ended with sessionInfo(), and its printout named the version of dplyr under “other attached packages”. Get the same version number with one line of code instead of reading it by eye.
blocks.answer:
packageVersion("dplyr")
[1] ‘1.1.4’

packageVersion(), from the section on packages, prints version 1.1.4. That is the same as dplyr_1.1.4 in the printout. Your own computer may print a newer version. Then your outputs may differ from this book’s, and the version line tells you why.

blocks.prompt: You want ten penguin rows picked at random, for a colleague to check against the field notebooks. She must get the same ten when she runs your script. Write the lines that pick ten row numbers from the penguin file with seed 52. Show that running them twice gives the same ten.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

set.seed(52)
first <- sample(nrow(penguins_raw), 10)
set.seed(52)
second <- sample(nrow(penguins_raw), 10)

first
identical(first, second)
 [1]  82 179 339 317 133 142  55 220 273 117
[1] TRUE

nrow(penguins_raw) is 344, so the picks are row numbers from 1 to 344. identical() asks whether two objects are exactly the same, and answers TRUE. In the script, set.seed(52) goes once, directly above the pick. The same ten come out for anyone who runs it on the same version of R.

blocks.prompt:
Meera’s script reports the mean body mass of the penguins. Earlier in the same session she had typed two lines in the console. Here is everything her session ran, and what it printed:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
penguins_raw <- read_csv(here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
penguins_raw <- penguins_raw |>
  filter(Island == "Biscoe")

Her script, code/analysis.R, run line by line in that session:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
penguins_raw |>
  summarise(mean_mass_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_mass_g
        <dbl>
1       4716.

She writes “mean body mass 4716 g” in her draft. What broke, and what is the right number for the whole file?
blocks.answer:
The script uses penguins_raw without making it. In her session that object was the Biscoe rows only, because of the second console line. So 4716 g is the mean for one island, and the script does not say so. It looks reasonable because it is a real mean of real penguins.

Save her script and run it as a stranger would:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
penguins_raw |>
  summarise(mean_mass_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE))
Rscript code/analysis.R
Error: object 'penguins_raw' not found
Execution halted

The fresh run finds the gap at once. Add the packages and the reading line to the script:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
penguins_raw <- read_csv(here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
penguins_raw |>
  summarise(mean_mass_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE))
Rscript code/analysis.R
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_mass_g
        <dbl>
1       4202.

About 4202 g for every row with a body mass, against 4716 g for Biscoe alone. If she wants Biscoe, the filter belongs in the script, where a reader can see it.

blocks.prompt:
Ravi checks his script before sending it. In his session the penguin file is already read. He runs the script with source(), sees no error, and tells his guide it is reproducible:

library(readr)
penguins_raw <- read_csv(here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
n_rows <- nrow(penguins_raw)
source(here::here("code", "analysis.R"))
n_rows
[1] 344

What is wrong with his check?
blocks.answer:
source() ran the script in Ravi’s own workspace, where penguins_raw already existed. So the check could not find the missing reading line. It looks like a test because the whole file ran without an error. But it ran with Ravi’s objects.

The test that counts starts from nothing:

n_rows <- nrow(penguins_raw)
Rscript code/analysis.R
Error: object 'penguins_raw' not found
Execution halted

The script needs library(readr) and the read_csv() line at its top. Then the same command runs to the end. source() is a fair test only straight after restarting R.

blocks.prompt: A thesis’s methods chapter says: “All analyses were performed in R and are fully reproducible.” The candidate gives you the project folder. Decide what to run to test the sentence, write it down, and then say what a successful run would still not establish.
blocks.answer:
Run the README’s command in a terminal, in the project folder, on your computer:

Rscript code/analysis.R

Then compare what lands in output/ with the tables in the thesis, number by number. Read the sessionInfo() printout at the end of the run against the versions the candidate recorded.

If the run reaches the last line and every number matches, you have shown one thing. The script reruns from the raw files on a second computer and gives the thesis’s numbers.

It does not establish:

  • that the numbers are right. A script can rerun perfectly and still compute the wrong thing;
  • that the raw files are the files that were collected. The run starts from whatever is in data-raw/;
  • that it will rerun next year. Newer package versions may stop it or change a result, unless the versions are pinned, which is renv’s job two rungs up;
  • that every number in the text came from the script. A number typed into the chapter by hand has no line of code behind it.

So the sentence the candidate can defend is narrower: “The analysis reruns from the raw data with one command, Rscript code/analysis.R, on R 4.3.3.”

blocks.prompt: In a department meeting a colleague says: “My script gives the same table every time. I ran it twice yesterday in RStudio and got the same numbers.” His script reads the penguin file and writes the number of rows of each sex to output/sex_counts.csv. Decide what would actually test his claim, run it, and say what your result does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Running twice in the same RStudio session tests nothing new: the second run had the first run’s workspace. The test is two runs that each start from nothing, with output/ deleted in between, and a comparison of the files. Here is his script:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(here)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)

sex_counts <- penguins_raw |>
  count(Sex)
write_csv(sex_counts, here("output", "sex_counts.csv"))

Run it and keep a copy of the output. Delete output/, run it again, and compare. cmp compares two files and prints nothing when they are the same. cp copies a file, rm -r deletes a folder, && runs the next command only if the last one succeeded, and echo prints its words:

Rscript code/analysis.R > /dev/null 2>&1
cp output/sex_counts.csv first_run.csv
rm -r output
Rscript code/analysis.R > /dev/null 2>&1
cmp first_run.csv output/sex_counts.csv && echo "identical"
cat output/sex_counts.csv
identical
Sex,n
FEMALE,165
MALE,168
NA,11

> /dev/null 2>&1 throws away what each run prints, since only the files matter here. The two files are identical: 165, 168 and 11 rows, which add up to 344.

What this does not establish:

  • that the script runs on his colleagues’ computers, with their package versions;
  • that the counts are right. They are the rows of the file, and the 11 rows with no sex recorded are counted as NA, not hidden;
  • anything about penguins beyond this file.

He can now say “the script gives the same table from a fresh start on my computer”. That is more than he could say before, and less than “it reproduces”.
